title: Gethsemane (Matthew 26:36–46)
hook: he asks the cup to pass, then not my will but thine; they fall asleep

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mandatum: at the last supper he knelt and washed their feet. Your line was as I have done to you. Tonight, a garden.

Supper is over. They sing a hymn and walk out of the city in the dark, down across a little valley and up into an olive grove on the far side. He tells most of them to sit and wait while he goes on to pray, and takes three with him: Peter, James and John. Then, Matthew says, he begins to grow sorrowful and to be sad, and he tells them so. In the Douay-Rheims: "My soul is sorrowful even unto death: stay you here, and watch with me." The one who calmed storms is asking his friends not to leave him alone. He goes a few steps further, falls on his face, and prays.
screen: `OUT OF THE CITY, IN THE DARK.` → `PETER, JAMES AND JOHN.` → `STAY YOU HERE, AND WATCH WITH ME.`

segments.voice: The name Gethsemane most likely comes from Aramaic words for an oil press, a place where olives were crushed until the oil ran out. Matthew doesn't explain the name; he goes straight to the prayer: "My Father, if it be possible, let this chalice pass from me. Nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt." The chalice, the cup, is an old biblical picture for what life pours out for you to drink; here it means the suffering coming at dawn. Notice he asks. He doesn't pretend he wants it. Luke even says his sweat fell like drops of blood. The Church teaches that Jesus had a real human will, and here you can hear it: a man who does not want to die, handing himself over anyway. Luke gives today's line, in the Douay-Rheims: "not my will, but thine be done." Then he walks back, and the three are asleep. "What? Could you not watch one hour with me?" He isn't furious. He almost makes excuses for them: "The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh weak." Three times he prays. Three times they sleep. Catholics keep that hour. On Holy Thursday night, after the evening Mass, the Blessed Sacrament is carried to a side altar, and people come to watch with him into the night. Tradition ties the holy hour, an hour of prayer before the Eucharist, to that same question.
screen: `AN OIL PRESS, WHERE OLIVES ARE CRUSHED.` · `LET THIS CHALICE PASS FROM ME.` · `A REAL HUMAN WILL, HANDED OVER.` · `COULD YOU NOT WATCH ONE HOUR?` · then, large: `NOT MY WILL, BUT THINE BE DONE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person carrying something heavy right now, an illness, a loss, a fear; you can't fix it, and that's not the job tonight. The job is only to stay: hold them in mind, and when you notice you've drifted to your own list, come back, the way he came back to his sleeping friends. If you pray, you can simply pray for them.
Gethsemane. The olive grove across the valley, whose name probably means oil press, where he prayed and his friends slept. Today's word.
Your line: not my will. He said what he wanted first, honestly. That's sixty-one days.

howItsDone: On Holy Thursday night Catholic parishes keep the Blessed Sacrament at an altar of repose so people can watch and pray with Jesus, and some Catholics keep a regular holy hour before the Eucharist.

chat.says: If Jesus was God, why did he pray in the garden not to suffer?
options: He had a real human will; he asked honestly, then said: not my will, but thine.
He was only testing his friends, to see whether they would stay awake.
He never felt afraid; he prayed that way just to set a good example.
chat.meaning: The Church teaches Jesus had a real human will. He asked for the chalice to pass, then handed himself over anyway.
